WhatsApp Stranger Scam UK: How to Spot and Stop It

A message from someone you don't recognise on WhatsApp can seem harmless—but it's often the start of a carefully planned scam.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-22 · 9 min read

WhatsApp scam UKWhatsApp stranger messageWhatsApp impersonation scam
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What is a WhatsApp stranger scam?

A WhatsApp stranger scam happens when someone you don't know—or someone pretending to be someone you do know—contacts you on WhatsApp and gradually builds a false relationship with you. The scammer's goal is to eventually ask for money, personal information, or access to your accounts. These scams are effective because WhatsApp feels more personal and trustworthy than email or SMS, and because the scammer can take time to build rapport before making their request. They may claim to be a friend in trouble, a business representative, a romantic interest, or someone offering a job or investment opportunity.

The scammer often uses a stolen or spoofed phone number, or a new number that looks similar to one you know. What makes these scams particularly dangerous is that they exploit the trust you naturally place in direct messaging—you're more likely to believe a WhatsApp message than a random email, which is exactly what the scammer is counting on.

Warning signs of a WhatsApp stranger scam

  • A message from someone claiming to be a friend or family member, but from a number you don't recognise or a slightly different number than usual. Ask yourself: would they really contact you from a new number without explaining why?
  • Urgent requests for money, often with an emotional story attached (a sick relative, a business emergency, a travel crisis). Genuine emergencies rarely happen via WhatsApp first.
  • Requests to move the conversation to a different app or platform, or to keep the conversation secret. Legitimate contacts don't usually ask you to hide things.
  • Offers that sound too good to be true: high-paying jobs with minimal qualifications, investment returns that are unusually generous, or romantic connections that develop very quickly. These are classic scammer tactics.
  • Requests for personal information like your date of birth, passport details, bank account numbers, or passwords. No legitimate business or friend needs these via WhatsApp.
  • Pressure to act quickly or threats of consequences if you don't comply. Scammers create artificial urgency to stop you thinking clearly.
  • Poor grammar, spelling mistakes, or an unusual tone compared to how the person normally writes. This is especially telling if it's supposedly someone you know well.
  • Requests to verify your identity by sending photos of documents, or to download an app or click a link to 'confirm' something. These are common ways scammers steal data or install malware.

How the scam unfolds: from first contact to the ask

The scam typically starts with a casual message from an unknown number. The scammer might say something like 'Hi, it's been a while' or 'I think you have the wrong number but let's chat anyway.' If you respond, they begin building a relationship—asking about your life, sharing stories, and gradually becoming more friendly. This phase can last days or even weeks, depending on how much time the scammer has and how engaged you are. During this time, they're learning about you: your job, your family, your financial situation, and your vulnerabilities.

Once they've established enough trust, they introduce their 'problem' or 'opportunity.' A scammer posing as a friend might say they're stuck abroad without access to their bank account and need you to send money urgently. One pretending to be a business might ask you to verify your account details or pay a fee. A romance scammer might eventually ask for money to visit you or to help with a supposed emergency. If you agree to send money, they'll provide bank details or ask you to use a money transfer app. Once the money is sent, they disappear.

If you've shared personal information, they may use it for identity theft or to target you further. The entire process is designed to feel natural and trustworthy, which is why so many people fall for it.

How to verify if a WhatsApp contact is really who they claim to be

If someone you know contacts you from a new or unfamiliar number, verify their identity before engaging further. The safest method is to call them on a number you already have for them—not a number they've given you in the message. If it's supposedly a friend or family member, ring them on their usual number and ask directly if they've been messaging you. If it's a business, go to their official website and use the contact number listed there, never one provided in the message.

Check the phone number itself: if it's from someone claiming to be a friend, does it match the country code you'd expect? Scammers often use numbers from outside the UK or numbers that look similar to legitimate ones but with one or two digits different. Look at their WhatsApp profile: does it have a profile picture? How long have they been on WhatsApp? A brand new account with no profile picture is a red flag.

If someone is asking you to verify your identity or account details, go directly to the official website or app of the organisation they claim to represent—don't use any links they've sent you. Be especially cautious of requests to download apps, click links, or move to a different platform; these are common ways scammers gain access to your device or data. Trust your instinct: if something feels off, it probably is.

What to do immediately if you've already engaged with a scammer

If you've been messaging with someone you now suspect is a scammer, stop communicating with them immediately and do not send any money. If you've already sent money, act fast: contact your bank or the money transfer service you used (such as Wise, PayPal, or your bank's app) right away and explain that you've been scammed. Many transfers can be stopped or reversed if you report them quickly, especially if the money hasn't been withdrawn yet.

If you've shared personal information like your date of birth, passport number, or bank details, contact your bank and ask them to monitor your account for suspicious activity. Consider placing a fraud alert on your credit file by contacting Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion—this makes it harder for someone to open accounts in your name. If you've clicked a link or downloaded an app the scammer sent you, run a full security scan on your phone using your device's built-in security tools or a reputable antivirus app.

Change your passwords for any accounts the scammer might have access to, starting with your email and banking apps. Do not delete the messages—you'll need them as evidence when you report the scam. Block the contact on WhatsApp and report them to WhatsApp itself by opening the chat, tapping the contact name, and selecting 'Report Contact.'

How to report a WhatsApp stranger scam in the UK

Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.org.uk. They'll log your report and pass it to the relevant authorities. If the scammer sent you a suspicious link or asked you to download something, report it to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) by forwarding the details to report@phishing.gov.uk. If you received the initial contact via SMS as well as WhatsApp, forward the SMS to 7726—this alerts your mobile network to the scam.

Report the contact directly to WhatsApp: open the chat, tap the contact name at the top, scroll down, and select 'Report Contact.' WhatsApp takes these reports seriously and may remove accounts engaged in scamming. If money was sent and you used your bank's app or a money transfer service, report it to them as well—they have fraud teams that can sometimes recover funds or prevent further transfers. You can also contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 for guidance on next steps and support.

If you believe your identity has been compromised, report it to Action Fraud (part of Report Fraud) as well. Keep records of all your reports, including reference numbers, as you may need them if the scammer tries to contact you again or if there are further consequences.

Frequently asked questions

Someone messaged me on WhatsApp saying they're my friend but from a different number—is this definitely a scam?

Not necessarily, but it's a common scam tactic. The safest approach is to call your friend on their usual number and ask if they've been messaging you. If they haven't, block the contact immediately. If they have, ask them why they're using a different number—there may be a legitimate reason, like a lost phone or a new SIM. Never send money or personal information based on a message from an unfamiliar number, even if the person claims to be someone you know.

I sent money to someone on WhatsApp before realising it was a scam—can I get it back?

Contact your bank or the money transfer service you used (such as your bank's app, Wise, or PayPal) immediately and explain that you've been scammed. If the money hasn't been withdrawn yet, there's a chance it can be stopped or reversed. The sooner you report it, the better your chances. You should also report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 and your bank's fraud team. Recovery isn't guaranteed, but acting quickly gives you the best chance.

What should I do if I've already shared my bank details or passport number with a WhatsApp scammer?

Contact your bank immediately and tell them you've shared your details with a scammer. Ask them to monitor your account for suspicious activity and consider freezing your account temporarily if necessary. Contact the three main credit reference agencies (Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion) and ask them to place a fraud alert on your credit file—this makes it harder for someone to open accounts in your name. Change your passwords for all your important accounts, especially your email and banking apps. You should also report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040. Monitor your credit report regularly for the next few months to catch any unauthorised activity early.

Can WhatsApp remove a scammer's account if I report them?

WhatsApp does take reports of scamming seriously and may remove accounts that are engaged in fraud or impersonation. To report a contact, open the chat with them, tap their name at the top, scroll down, and select 'Report Contact.' However, WhatsApp's response time varies, and they don't always notify you of the outcome. Reporting to WhatsApp is important, but you should also report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) and your bank so that the wider authorities are aware and can investigate.

Is it safe to block someone on WhatsApp if I think they're a scammer?

Yes, blocking is safe and recommended. When you block someone on WhatsApp, they can no longer see your profile picture, status, or online status, and they can't message or call you. Block the contact immediately if you suspect it's a scam. However, don't delete the chat before reporting it—you'll need the messages as evidence when you report the scam to Report Fraud or your bank. After you've reported it and saved any evidence you need, you can safely delete the conversation.
